extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and critics of poetics and classical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards (from Aristotle via commentary) for judging epic and tragic poetry: when poetic 'absurdities' are permissible, how to assess subject/means/manner, and the comparative merits of tragedy and epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdities may be justified by established solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: All that appears absurd may be also justified by certain ways (Aristotle gives a set of principal solutions) so that apparent absurdities in poets can often be defended rather than condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentator notes Aristotle's claim that there are 'twelve' principal solutions (with many particulars related to them). Examples: Homeric fictions (Thetis promising to perfume Patroclus to prevent corruption; Sleep and the Graces as a poetic way to denote spring/renewal). To defend an apparent absurdity, bring to bear these established poetic devices and seek proximate places/meanings rather than dismissing it as mere improbability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not resort to impossibilities without necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet is inexcuable when, without any necessity, he has recourse to impossibilities or absurdities, creates bad characters, contradicts himself, or violates the rules of his art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limit: poetic licence does not permit arbitrary impossibilities. Critics should separate excusable poetic devices from genuine errors where improbability is needless and harms character or action (examples: gratuitous improbable incidents in Euripides' Medea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics' objections reduce to three heads: Subject, Means, Manner
rubrics_metrics.description: All criticisms of poets can be classified under three main categories: (1) the Subject, (2) the Means (les moyens), and (3) the Manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames defenses and answers by locating the objection in one of these three domains; further subdivisions (see separate rubric entries) give the specific modes of justification appropriate to each head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-related defenses (four kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: For objections about the subject there are roughly four ways of examining/defending: (a) what it is, (b) what it ought to be, (c) what is said to be, (d) what it may be according to extensive probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the complaint is about the subject-matter (e.g., scale of Homer's shield, universe depicted on it), consider whether the poet's design/intention, conventional subject-treatment, or broader probable sense justify the depiction rather than literal factual plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-related defenses (five means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to the means of expression may be answered by reference to five devices: the Metaphor, the Foreign Word, the Accent, the Pointing, and the Ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These linguistic/style devices can legitimately produce forms that at first seem odd or improper; critics should assess whether the device is purposeful and appropriate to effect rather than calling it mere error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner-related defenses (three tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the objection concerns manner, examine: (1) if the fault is proper (appropriate) or not, (2) if the thing is the same or different (contextual identity), (3) if it is always the same character (consistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these tests to determine whether apparent contradictions or oddities stem from acceptable variation of manner vs. real inconsistency or mischaracterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the poet's design/intention before judging
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics must take pains to instruct themselves about the poet's intention; many apparent faults disappear once one understands the design (e.g., Homer's shield intends to represent the universe and occupations of men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: critics who thought Homer's shield too 'charged' failed to appreciate its intended scope (covering a whole man, representing the universe). Always ask what the poet intended to represent and whether the form serves that design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow general opinion (fame) only if not contradicted by better truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet ought to follow common/general opinion, but that opinion must be general and not simultaneously contradicted by better-explained truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legitimizes conventional or mythic representations (e.g., treatment of gods) provided that they accord with widely held beliefs or are not refuted by superior known facts or explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine apparent contradictions as logical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Places that seem contrary to what the poet has said elsewhere should be examined 'as we do objections in logic' to find solutions (identity of speaker, different times/seasons, contextual meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for resolutions in context: speaker change, temporal change, rhetorical device, or broader probable meaning. Compare passages to reveal hidden coherence (examples include Juno/Sleep episodes in Homer and Virgil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not condemn a poem for actors' or readers' faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is not responsible for the defects of the actor or reader; performance faults (bad gestures, pronunciation, reading) do not make the written work itself bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text's merit should be judged independently of contemporary performances; the faults of actors (e.g., lascivious gestures) may spoil a representation but are not faults of the poet's composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures and motions are permissible but must suit dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions/gestures/dance are not blameworthy per se; they are to be condemned only when lascivious, effeminate, or disagreeable to the poem's majesty. Ancient poets directed gestures and steps to ensure dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should prescribe or ensure gestures and choreography that are noble and consistent with the verses; they may model gestures on statuary and ancient dances to preserve propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing unnecessary bad or irrelevant characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing a bad character without occasion is a fault (e.g., the gratuitous appearance of Aegeus in Euripides' Medea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each character should have a necessary role in the action; extraneous personages that neither affect the plot nor arise from necessity count as real defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and compactness favor tragedy over dispersed epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy preserves unity better than epic; a well-compacted imitation (unity of action, brevity appropriate to effect) is more agreeable and affects the audience more sensibly than a diffuse, long epic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an imitation attempted to include many actions/incidents it loses perfect unity (contrast Homeric epics, which contain multiple parts each near-perfect). Compactness and unity are marks of excellence (example: Sophocles' Oedipus compactness vs. prolonged diffusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of excellence: relative simplicity / least need of external aid
rubrics_metrics.description: That imitation which requires the least external aid or assistance (simpler in means) is, other things equal, the more perfect; simplicity in obtaining the poetic end is a sign of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle compares epic to excellent flute-players (who need only sound) vs. bad players who add gestures; this 'least aid' test is used to compare epic and tragedy, though other advantages of tragedy (see below) complicate the judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy attains poetic ends more exactly and offers richer modes (music, decoration, action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy may be preferable because it produces its effect more exactly and has advantages (hexameter can be used, music, decoration, evidence of action) that increase its pleasure and efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy can include everything epic has and more; it gives a more immediate, sensibly moving experience and can combine verbal art with spectacle and music to achieve its intended emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic imagination (ingenium) may go beyond mere representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic art often presents more than what is literally seen; there is 'more understood than is painted' — ingenuity surpasses mere art or literal depiction (e.g., Apelles painting thunder, TImanthes' works had 'something more understood than seen').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should allow for imaginative enhancement: poets may depict events, emotions, and universe-scale designs that transcend straightforward realism, provided they cohere with design and probability.
